title: The cave (1 Samuel 24)
hook: David could kill Saul while he sleeps, and cuts only the edge of his robe
carry: I will not lift my hand

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonathan's love: a robe, a sword, an arrow shot beyond a boy. Your line was a friend closer than a brother. What did you give? Day seven hundred eighteen.

Dark, cool, and very quiet. David and his men are crouched in the back of a cave in the wilderness of En-gedi, among the wild goats' rocks. Outside, King Saul is hunting him with an army. And then the king himself walks in, alone, to relieve himself, and has no idea who is sitting in the dark behind him. David's men can hardly breathe. One of them whispers what they're all thinking: this is the day the Lord promised, your enemy delivered into your hand. Do to him whatever seems good to you. David gets up. He creeps forward with a blade. And what he does next is today.

He cuts off a corner of Saul's robe. That's all. The king walks back out into the light and never feels it. And then a strange line, in the King James Bible: "David's heart smote him, because he had cut off Saul's skirt." Not for sparing him. For the cloth. Even that small cut felt like too much. He turns to his men and stops them cold: "The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the LORD's anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him." Anointed is the key word. Saul was anointed king with oil, and David will not be the one to remove him, even after spears thrown at his head, even with a promise of the throne. Then David does something brave. He walks out of the cave after Saul and calls to him. He bows to the ground. He holds up the corner of the robe as proof: I was close enough to kill you, and I didn't. In his words: "I will not put forth mine hand against my lord; for he is the LORD's anointed." He leaves the judging to God. And Saul, the hunter, breaks. "Is this thy voice, my son David? And Saul lifted up his voice, and wept." He says it plainly: "Thou art more righteous than I." It doesn't last. Saul will hunt David again. The cave doesn't fix their story. What it shows is a man with every excuse and every chance, choosing not to take it. Some Christians read this chapter beside Jesus's teaching to love enemies and Paul's line in Romans about leaving vengeance to God. The robe corner is the whole lesson: proof of what you could have done.

For the next two minutes, find one chance to get even, and set it down. Breathe out slowly first. Let your mind go to someone who has wronged you, in a small way or a large one. Notice the chance you have, or could make: a remark you could repeat, a favor you could withhold, a story you could tell. Notice how sharp the blade is. Then picture David lowering his hand, holding only a scrap of cloth. You don't have to forgive everything today. Just decide not to cut. If you pray, you can hand the judging to God in silence. The bell holds the time.
The cave. In the dark at En-gedi, David spares the king who is hunting him, and takes only the corner of his robe.
Your line: I will not lift my hand. Today, when the chance to get even shows up, let it walk back out of the cave. Day seven hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Some Christians read David sparing Saul in the cave alongside Jesus's teaching to love one's enemies, and the story is told in sermons and Sunday schools about refusing revenge.

original.note: Hebrew: anointed. David will not lift his hand against the LORD's anointed (1 Samuel 24:6).

trapdoor: what you thought: David sneaks up on a sleeping king.
what it means: in this cave Saul is awake (the sleeping scene comes in chapter 26); David takes only a corner of his robe, and even that troubles him.
what a scholar hears: Saul is the LORD's mashiach, anointed; David leaves judgment to God, and the robe's corner is proof of mercy.

notes: The index hook says Saul 'sleeps'; in 1 Samuel 24 Saul goes into the cave 'to cover his feet' (24:3), usually read as relieving himself, and the text does not say he slept (the sleeping scene is 1 Samuel 26). The script follows chapter 24; consider correcting the index hook.
'Spears thrown at his head' refers to 1 Samuel 18:10–11 and 19:10.
The link to Matthew 5:44 and Romans 12:19 is presented as how Christians have read the chapter; confirm.
Saul resumes the pursuit in 1 Samuel 26; stated generally ('later in 1 Samuel').
Original: מָשִׁיחַ as the noun 'anointed'; in 24:6 the form is מְשִׁיחַ (construct). Confirm the note's wording.
Editor: howItsDone's 'Christians often read' and 'a common story' softened to 'some Christians' and 'is told' (no source for frequency); practice 'feel how sharp' changed to 'notice'.

Audit: practice opening varied (every day in the run opened 'Here's the practice: ... Settle, and breathe.'); trapdoor now separates chapter 24 (Saul awake, in the cave) from chapter 26 (Saul asleep), since the index hook conflates them.
